title: Riven ash stool leg
subtitle: A drawknife-shaved leg for a four-legged rustic stool
excerpt: A stool leg in green ash, riven from a section of log and shaved to a taper on the shaving horse. The riven surface follows the grain, making a stronger leg than a sawn one. Four legs of this type, fitted into a seat board, make a stool that will outlast most furniture.
sourceNotes: John Alexander, Make a Chair from a Tree (1978), public-domain technique descriptions; adapted for ash stool legs following the Welsh stick-chair tradition.

glossaryTerms.definition: Freshly felled or recently riven wood, still high in moisture content. Carves easily under hand tools.
Splitting wood along the grain using a froe and mallet rather than sawing across it. Riven surfaces follow the grain and are stronger than sawn surfaces.
A cleaving tool with a blade set at right angles to its handle. Struck with a mallet to split wood along the grain.
A foot-operated clamp bench for holding work while using a drawknife or spokeshave.

content.text: A stool leg in
green wood
ash,
riven

from the log and shaved to a taper on the shaving horse. Riving follows the grain: the fibres stay intact end to end. Sawn legs cut across the grain wherever it wanders. The green ash shaves easily, and the leg shrinks tight into its seat socket as it dries.
Before you start cutting.
Froe and mallet: keep the striking face of the mallet on the spine of the froe, not the blade. The froe blade is not designed to be struck on its edge.
Drawknife: the drawknife is pulled toward the body. Control the bevel angle and the stopping point. Never allow the blade to travel past the thigh.
Shaving horse: the foot pedal must lock the work before the drawknife stroke begins. If the work moves under a drawknife stroke, stop and reset the clamp.
Workspace: stable ground underfoot. Loose or uneven footing under the shaving horse is a significant hazard with drawknife work.
First aid: keep a styptic pencil, gauze, and a clean dressing within reach. Apply firm pressure, elevate, and dress. A cut that shows fat or won't close with pressure goes to A&E, not a plaster.
Wood

Green ash from a section of straight, branch-free trunk, 30 to 35 cm in diameter, cut in winter when the sap is low. The section should be 50 cm long for a finished leg of 38 to 40 cm. Each quarter of the cross-section becomes one leg; four legs from one round section is the standard yield for a stool this size. Ash is the preferred species for legs because it is strong, splits cleanly, and bends under steam if a curved leg is needed for a future project.
Tools
Froe: for the initial riving of the log section.
Beetle mallet: for driving the froe.
Shaving horse: to hold each billet during drawknife work.
Drawknife, straight: for shaving the leg to a taper.
Spokeshave, flat (optional): for final smoothing of the taper.
Leather strop: strop the drawknife every thirty minutes of use.
Method
Step 1: Quarter the log
Stand the log section on end on a stable splitting block. Use the
froe

and beetle mallet to split the round section first in half, then each half in half again. Position the froe on the top face of the end grain, passing through the centre of the log. Strike the spine of the froe with the mallet to drive the blade in, then lever the handle to open the split.
Step 2: Remove the pith

The pith (the soft centre of the log) is in one of the four quarters. Rive that quarter again to remove the pith section. The pith is weak and shrinks unpredictably as the wood dries; any leg section containing pith should be discarded or used only for practice.
Step 3: Drawknife the leg to shape
Mount the quarter billet in the
shaving horse

with the top of the leg away from you and the bottom nearest. Use the drawknife with the bevel up (bevel-up gives a slicing cut in green ash; bevel-down removes more material per stroke). Work from the top toward the bottom to shape the leg to a round taper: 38 mm diameter at the tenon end, increasing to 50 mm at the seat end.
Step 4: Cut the tenon

The top of the leg (the narrow end) is turned or shaved to a 22 mm tenon, 35 mm long, that fits into a drilled hole in the seat board. The tenon is cut slightly oversize and driven in while both tenon and seat are green; as they dry, the tenon shrinks and the seat hole shrinks around it, locking the joint without glue.
Finishing

Green ash legs are left unfinished until fully dry: typically six to eight weeks in a warm room. Once dry, apply raw linseed oil to all surfaces. One coat, left to soak in for one hour, wiped dry. The cure time for raw linseed on a structural piece is two weeks. The leg sees no food contact and the two-week cure is sufficient for furniture use.

attrs.symptom: The froe is running off to one side rather than splitting straight
attrs.cause: The grain in the log is not perfectly straight; the froe follows the grain rather than the intended split line.
attrs.fix: Lever the froe handle toward the direction you want the split to run. Lever gently; force closes the split and traps the froe. Work slowly.

attrs.symptom: The drawknife is chattering across the surface rather than cutting
attrs.cause: The bevel angle is too shallow or the edge is dull.
attrs.fix: Strop the drawknife. Check the bevel: bevel-up should produce a clean slicing cut in green ash at a 15 to 20 degree presentation angle.

attrs.cause: The pith was included in the tenon section.
attrs.fix: Check all billets for pith before shaving the tenon section. Discard any billet where the pith is within 15 mm of the tenon centre.
